properties.natural_language: When SELFDESTRUCT is encountered during contract execution, the executing contract state must be accessible and the current transaction context must be identifiable to determine if the contract was created in the same transaction.

After checking if a contract was created in the same transaction where SELFDESTRUCT is called, if true, the contract state must be completely deleted; if false, only the balance must be transferred while preserving the contract code and storage.
A contract that persists after SELFDESTRUCT (not created in same transaction) must maintain all storage slots and code unchanged, with only the balance transferred to the beneficiary address.
After SELFDESTRUCT execution completes, if the contract was destroyed (same-transaction creation), the EVM execution must halt successfully with the contract state marked as destroyed.
When checking refund eligibility for SELFDESTRUCT, if the operation is not eligible for refund, EIP-2929 access list rules must be applied for gas accounting instead of legacy refund mechanisms.

When SELFDESTRUCT targets itself (beneficiary == contract address) and burn conditions are enabled, the ether balance must be burned rather than transferred, resulting in permanent removal from total supply.
When a transaction is received for validation in Prague fork, the transaction type field must be checked against supported types before proceeding with contract creation or fee structure validation.
If transaction type validation fails or contract creation validation fails, the transaction must be rejected with a specific error before fee structure checks are performed.
After fee structure validation, if max fee is insufficient or priority fee exceeds max fee, the transaction must be rejected before execution with appropriate fee-related error codes.
For blob transactions, if blob gas limit is exceeded, blob fee is insufficient, versioned hash is invalid, or blob data does not exist, the transaction must be rejected before inclusion in a block.
When contract creation is initiated, if the init code size exceeds the maximum allowed limit, the creation must fail before code execution begins.
For authorization list transactions, if the authorization list is empty when required, the transaction must be rejected with an empty authorization list error.

When a wire protocol message is received from a peer over the network boundary, the message type must be validated before processing to determine if it is supported in the current protocol version (eth/67).
After protocol upgrade from eth/66 to eth/67, the GetNodeData and NodeData messages must be disabled and any attempt to use them must result in rejection or deprecation handling.
When a deprecated message type is received (GetNodeData or NodeData), the message must be rejected and not processed, with the connection potentially maintained for backward compatibility.
When state data is needed and the peer supports only eth/67, Snap protocol messages (GetBytecodes or GetTrieNodes) must be used instead of the deprecated GetNodeData message.

Throughout the protocol migration from eth/66 to eth/67, state data requests must always result in a response (either via GetNodeData for eth/66 peers or Snap protocol for eth/67 peers), ensuring backward compatibility during the transition period.

When the execution layer receives a forkchoice_updated notification from the consensus layer via the Engine API boundary, the fork choice state must include valid head, safe, and finalized block hashes before processing.

When fetching PoW block data from external sources during merge transition validation, the terminal PoW block hash and total difficulty must be verifiable against the configured terminal total difficulty threshold.

After detecting a merge block, validation must confirm either the terminal PoW block conditions (total difficulty threshold reached) or a terminal block override configuration before transitioning to post-merge state.

After fork choice computation, the safe block must be computed and the execution layer must be notified via forkchoice_updated, potentially triggering chain reorganization and finalized payload persistence.

When proposing reorg conditions are evaluated (head late, proposer slot timing, FFG competitive), if any condition fails, fork choice must proceed normally; if all pass and weak head with strong parent is detected, fork choice may be suppressed for reorg opportunity.
When a required PoW block is unavailable during merge transition validation, block processing must be deferred until the PoW block becomes available, preventing invalid state transitions.

After the merge transition is completed and post-merge state is established, all subsequent blocks must be validated as execution payloads from the consensus layer, and PoW validation must not be performed.

When a JSON-RPC client submits a request over the boundary to the Ethereum node, the request must contain a valid JSON-RPC 2.0 structure with method, params, and id fields before method-specific validation occurs.

When a client submits a raw transaction via eth_sendRawTransaction across the trust boundary, the raw transaction bytes must be valid RLP-encoded transaction data before signature verification and nonce checking.

After a filter is created (eth_newFilter, eth_newBlockFilter, eth_newPendingTransactionFilter), if the filter is not accessed within the implementation-defined timeout period, it must be automatically removed and subsequent queries must return filter not found errors.

When gas estimation is performed via eth_estimateGas, if the transaction would revert, the RPC implementation may either return an error or return the gas limit required for execution up to the revert point, depending on implementation choices.

When querying pending block state (eth_getBlockByNumber with 'pending' tag), the returned data must represent the node's current view of the next block being assembled, but this state may be inconsistent across calls during active block construction.

If rate limiting is implemented for JSON-RPC requests, when the rate limit is exceeded, the server must return an error response (typically 429 Too Many Requests or JSON-RPC error) rather than silently dropping requests.

All JSON-RPC responses must conform to JSON-RPC 2.0 specification structure, containing either a result field (on success) or an error field (on failure), along with the matching request id, ensuring client-server communication integrity.
After Pectra fork activation occurs, both execution layer and consensus layer clients must recognize the new fork and activate all associated EIPs simultaneously to maintain consensus.
During Pectra fork activation, if networking improvements are marked as optional, nodes may activate the fork with or without implementing optional networking features without breaking consensus.

When execution layer and consensus layer activate Pectra features, if timing misalignment occurs (one layer activates before the other due to different trigger conditions), the node must handle the intermediate state without chain halts or consensus failures.

Throughout Pectra fork activation and afterward, the execution layer and consensus layer must maintain bidirectional communication and state consistency, with Engine API calls continuing to function correctly under the new fork rules.

When a provider event listener is registered for a specific event name, if a listener for the same event and callback already exists, the implementation may either allow duplicate registration or silently deduplicate, depending on implementation choices.

When attempting to remove a provider event listener that does not exist (mismatched event name or callback), the operation must complete without error, either silently succeeding or logging a warning without throwing exceptions.

When a provider event is emitted, all registered listeners for that event name must be invoked with the event data, and event names must be matched using case-sensitive comparison to ensure correct listener routing.

The provider event system must maintain a security boundary where malicious or compromised event listeners cannot affect the execution of other listeners or the underlying provider state, ensuring isolation between event handlers.

When a deposit Merkle proof is received from the Eth1 deposit contract boundary, the proof must be validated against the known deposit root and deposit count before processing the deposit for validator activation.

When a beacon block proposal is received from a validator proposer across the network boundary, the block signature must be verified against the proposer's public key and the block must pass all state transition function validations before acceptance.

After processing epoch transitions, validator activation and exit queues must be processed respecting the churn limit (MAX_PER_EPOCH_ACTIVATION_CHURN_LIMIT), which may vary based on network configuration and total active validator count.

During Eth1 data voting in beacon block processing, if no Eth1 data receives majority votes within the voting period (EPOCHS_PER_ETH1_VOTING_PERIOD), the previous Eth1 data must be retained for deposit processing continuity.

When processing a deposit with an invalid BLS signature in the deposit data, the deposit must still be included in the beacon state deposit queue but the validator must not be activated, preventing loss of deposited ETH while maintaining security.

Throughout the beacon chain state transition, the total active validator balance must be updated correctly, and validator effective balances must be capped at MAX_EFFECTIVE_BALANCE regardless of actual balance, ensuring consistent weight calculations.

All beacon block state transitions must be deterministic and reproducible, such that any node processing the same block with the same pre-state will arrive at the identical post-state, ensuring global consensus.

When a block is received from the network for fork choice processing, the block must be validated for structural correctness and signature validity before being considered as a candidate in the fork choice algorithm.

When an attestation is received from a validator attester across the network boundary for fork choice weight calculation, the attestation signature and aggregation bits must be verified before incorporating the vote into the fork choice store.

After calculating proposer boost for the fork choice head, the boost weight must be computed as a committee weight with appropriate rounding, and implementations may differ in rounding strategies (floor, ceiling, or banker's rounding) without breaking consensus if within acceptable tolerances.

When processing attestations in the fork choice on_attestation handler, if the target block of the attestation is not yet in the fork choice store, the attestation may optionally be cached for later processing or discarded, depending on implementation buffering strategies.

When a reorganization exceeds a certain depth threshold (deep reorg), the node may reject the reorganization or apply additional validation checks to prevent long-range attacks, with the specific depth threshold being implementation-defined.

The fork choice head must always be the leaf block in the block tree with the greatest weight according to the LMD-GHOST algorithm, and this head must be on a chain that includes the latest justified and finalized checkpoints.

Across all protocol layers (execution, consensus, networking), cryptographic signatures must use the appropriate domain separation and signature schemes (ECDSA for execution layer transactions, BLS for consensus layer messages) to prevent cross-protocol signature replay attacks.

All state transitions resulting from untrusted input (network messages, RPC requests, user transactions) must be validated before application, with validation failures resulting in explicit rejection rather than silent state corruption.
The transaction context must accurately track whether a contract was created in the current transaction to enable correct SELFDESTRUCT behavior determination.
Same-transaction contract creation detection must be reliable and not subject to manipulation through complex call patterns or delegate calls.
Ether balance transfers from SELFDESTRUCT must complete atomically with the operation, preventing partial state where balance is deducted but not credited to beneficiary.
Transaction validation must occur before execution state changes, ensuring invalid transactions cannot partially modify state.
Exception handling for new transaction types must be backward compatible, ensuring older clients reject unknown types rather than misinterpreting them.
Protocol version negotiation must occur during connection establishment, allowing both peers to agree on supported message types before message exchange.
Deprecated message handling must maintain network connectivity during transition period, preventing network fragmentation between eth/66 and eth/67 implementations.
State synchronization functionality must remain available throughout the protocol transition, with Snap protocol providing equivalent or superior capabilities to deprecated GetNodeData.
Terminal total difficulty must be configured consistently across all nodes before merge activation to ensure unified merge transition.
Fork choice updates via Engine API must be processed atomically, with execution layer state consistent with consensus layer view after notification.
Block validation must not proceed when dependent PoW blocks are unavailable, maintaining validation integrity during merge transition.
JSON-RPC requests must be authenticated and authorized according to node policy before processing, preventing unauthorized access to sensitive methods.
Transaction submission via RPC must validate transaction data integrity before propagation to prevent malformed transactions from entering the mempool.
Filter lifecycle management must prevent resource exhaustion through automatic cleanup of expired filters based on implementation-defined timeout policies.
Pending block queries must return consistent data within reasonable time windows, though exact consistency guarantees are implementation-specific during active mining.
Fork activation epoch/block must be configured identically across execution and consensus layers to ensure synchronized activation.
Optional networking features in Pectra must not affect consensus validity, allowing nodes with different networking implementations to maintain chain consensus.
Execution and consensus layer fork activation must complete within acceptable timing tolerances to prevent prolonged inconsistent states.
Engine API communication must remain functional throughout fork activation, maintaining coordination between execution and consensus layers.
Event listener registration must validate callback functions to prevent registration of invalid or malicious handlers.
Event listener removal operations must be idempotent, safely handling removal of non-existent listeners without state corruption.
Event name matching must be case-sensitive and exact to ensure listeners receive only intended events and prevent cross-event interference.
Validator churn limits must be enforced consistently to prevent rapid changes in validator set that could destabilize consensus.
Eth1 data voting must converge to a single value within the voting period to ensure deposit processing continuity.
Invalid deposit signatures must not prevent deposit inclusion in state, preserving depositor funds while preventing validator activation with invalid credentials.
Deposit Merkle proofs must be validated against trusted Eth1 deposit contract state to prevent fraudulent validator activation.
Proposer boost calculation must use consistent rounding methods across implementations to prevent fork choice divergence.
Attestations for unknown blocks must be handled gracefully through caching or discarding to prevent fork choice store corruption.
Deep reorganization protection must activate at implementation-defined thresholds to prevent long-range attacks while allowing legitimate reorgs.
All data crossing trust boundaries (RPC requests, wire protocol messages, Engine API calls, network blocks, attestations, deposits, block proposals) must undergo validation before state modification.
Boundary validation failures must result in explicit rejection with appropriate error codes, never silent failure or partial state modification.
State transitions across all protocol components (EVM execution, transaction validation, consensus state, fork choice) must be atomic, with failed transitions resulting in complete rollback.
Cross-layer state consistency (execution-consensus) must be maintained through Engine API coordination, with no layer proceeding independently beyond acceptable timing bounds.
Resource exhaustion attacks must be prevented through gas limits (execution), rate limiting (RPC), filter cleanup (RPC), churn limits (consensus), and deep reorg protection (fork choice).
Signature verification must occur before trust is established for all signed data (transactions, blocks, attestations, deposits), using appropriate cryptographic schemes per layer.

Protocol upgrades (Prague fork, Pectra fork, eth/67 transition, merge activation) must maintain backward compatibility or provide explicit rejection of incompatible operations to prevent network fragmentation.

Error conditions must be handled deterministically across implementations, with ambiguous error cases (filter timeout, gas estimation, pending state, listener removal) documented and consistently implemented within deployment contexts.

All consensus-critical operations (block validation, state transition, fork choice, finalization) must be deterministic and produce identical results across all compliant implementations given identical inputs.
Data encoding and decoding (RLP for transactions, SSZ for consensus, JSON for RPC) must be validated for correctness before processing to prevent malformed data attacks.

Finalized state (finalized execution payloads, finalized beacon blocks, finalized checkpoints) must be immutable and persistent, with finality guarantees maintained across restarts and synchronization.
The EDGE-FETCH-POW-BLOCK boundary must validate PoW block data integrity before use in merge transition validation, preventing reliance on corrupted or manipulated historical PoW data.
When a contract execution reaches STATE-EXECUTION-HALTED after SELFDESTRUCT, all subsequent calls to the destroyed contract in the same transaction must encounter the destroyed state consistently.
STATE-MESSAGE-TYPE-VALID messages in the wire protocol must be processed completely and successfully, with processing failures treated as protocol violations rather than silent drops.

When ACTION-INITIATE-PAYLOAD-BUILD is triggered after forkchoice update, the payload building must respect all execution layer constraints including gas limit, base fee, and transaction validity for the target slot.

All transitions through EDGE-SAME-TX-TRUE and EDGE-SAME-TX-FALSE must be mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, ensuring every SELFDESTRUCT operation takes exactly one path based on creation context.

The complete validation flow from STATE-BLOB-TX-RECEIVED through blob gas, fee, versioned hash, and data existence checks must all pass for STATE-BLOB-TX-VALIDATED to be reached, with any single failure causing transaction rejection.

The proposer reorg suppression logic (checking head lateness, proposer slot timing, FFG competitiveness, finalization status, and weak head/strong parent) must evaluate all conditions sequentially, with fork choice suppression only occurring when all conditions pass.
